title: The 1977 Women's Conference That Changed America
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (Chuck is addressed as "iHeart Intro" in the transcript) examine the 1977 National Women's Conference in Houston, Texas (November 18-21, 1977), the federally funded gathering that produced a platform of planks on women's issues. They cover its origins in the 1975 International Women's Year and Ford's executive order, the state conferences and delegate selection, the inclusion of women of color, lesbians and conservatives, the Black Women's Plan of Action, the abortion and Department of Women's Affairs votes, and the conservative counter-rally led by Lottie Beth Hobbs and Phyllis Schlafly, which helped galvanize the religious right and the modern Republican coalition. They close with the limited federal follow-through under President Carter and a listener mail segment.

entities.name: Women Who Want to Be Women

segments.title: Opening and overview of the 1977 Houston conference
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the National Women's Conference in Houston, November 18-21, 1977, and Gloria Steinem's description of it as an important overlooked event.

segments.title: Religious right origins and the Stop ERA opposition
segments.summary: Discussion of how the conference is linked to the rise of the religious right, opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment, and Phyllis Schlafly and her Stop ERA group, including a backronym aside.

segments.title: Tangent on the Stop ERA name and acronym critique
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Stop ERA being a backronym and rate it as unnecessary, with a brief detour to a Dragnet-related production company sound effect.

segments.title: Origins: International Women's Year and Ford's commission
segments.summary: Ford's 1975 executive order creating the National Commission on the Observance of International Women's Year and its roughly five million dollar funding, plus the state conference process and Time's 1975 Woman of the Year coverage.

segments.title: Delegate selection and inclusive planning
segments.summary: Bella Abzug and organizers planned about two thousand delegates, with childcare and fee support to include farmers, minority women and other underrepresented groups.

segments.title: Feminist infighting and the coalition
segments.summary: Discussion of divisions within feminism, Betty Friedan's objection to the lesbian contingent, and how conservative opposition helped unite feminist groups.

segments.title: Conservative opposition organizing and abortion as a unifying issue
segments.summary: The IWY Citizens Review Committee and the coalition of Catholics, Mormons, evangelicals; inclusion of abortion rights as a catalyst; the Republican platform and Roe v. Wade.

segments.title: Conservative delegates, Mississippi men and Houston choice
segments.summary: Conservative delegates from states such as Utah and Mississippi, the male delegates from Mississippi, and the Higgins connection; Houston chosen as host city with Barbara Jordan and a Woman's Advocate office.

segments.title: Prominent speakers and Houston's politics
segments.summary: Notable attendees including Gloria Steinem, Coretta Scott King, Shirley Chisholm and Barbara Jordan; Maya Angelou's poem; the Texas governor's National Family Week and Houston's cut to the women's advocate office.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Torch relay and opening gatherings
segments.summary: Torch relay modeled on Seneca Falls from 1848 to Houston, national media coverage, and the first ladies appearing together.

segments.title: The conference planks
segments.summary: The final platform covered arts, childcare, credit, rape, reproductive freedom, sexual preference, and many other areas.

segments.title: Conservative delegates and the majority pins
segments.summary: Conservative delegates were called antis and wore majority pins; Lucy Kamaras reported that many were not in lockstep with the conservative platform.

segments.title: Black Women's Plan of Action and racial inclusion
segments.summary: Women of color pushed for the Black Women's Plan of Action to replace the minority resolution; Coretta Scott King presented it and it passed overwhelmingly; other women of color delegates were included.

segments.title: Lesbian rights plank and Betty Friedan's reversal
segments.summary: Gay and lesbian inclusion in the platform passed overwhelmingly; Betty Friedan publicly endorsed it, reversing her earlier position.

segments.title: Music tangent and parenthetical song titles
segments.summary: Lighthearted banter about the Gatlin Brothers and parenthetical song titles.

segments.title: Reproductive freedom plank and Department of Women's Affairs vote
segments.summary: Abortion funding plank passed while conservative delegates protested with a fetus image; the cabinet-level Department of Women's Affairs proposal was voted down after some feminists joined the conservatives in opposition.

segments.title: Lottie Beth Hobbs and the pro-family counter-rally
segments.summary: Hobbs' Women Who Want to Be Women led a counter-rally across town with Nellie Gray and NOMAM support, drawing around fifteen thousand; Schlafly spoke; attention from press and Republican Party.

segments.title: Aftermath: Carter response and legacy
segments.summary: Carter endorsed many goals, extended ERA ratification to 1982, and supported the Hyde Amendment; assessments found limited federal results but grassroots and coalition gains; Hosts discuss polarization and the coalition's effect on the Reagan era.

segments.title: Independent voters and closing remarks
segments.summary: Brief discussion of how the conference pulled in some Republican-leaning women and of independent voters, with a light exchange on the hosts' views.

segments.title: Listener mail from Beatrix
segments.summary: An eighth grader from McMinnville, Oregon, writes about the Rock Paper Scissors app, asks for an ADHD episode, and wishes luck in high school; hosts offer Portland show guest list tickets and shout out tech stuff.

segments.summary: Email address for listener mail and iHeartRadio credit.
